utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I begin by asking the Registrar to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-81-PT, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mark Harmon, Faith Devine and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And for Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Novak Lukic and I'm co-counsel for Mr. Perisic, together with me is Tina Drolec our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. The accused is not present. I understand you have something to say about his waiver.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yesterday, I got in contact with Mr. Perisic. He authorised me over the telephone to inform you that he is agreeable with today's Status Conference being held in his absence. And today we shall submit a written statement to confirm that consent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. I am to express my sympathy to the accused and to ask that you transmit that sympathy, Mr. Lukic, on the passing of his brother. At the same time, I feel the Tribunal is to be congratulated on having a system of provisional release that is sufficiently humanitarian in outlook to allow accused like Mr. Perisic to visit their relatives while ill, and I know that he was able to visit his brother while he was ill.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since we're talking about that, I would like to convey his gratitude to the Tribunal for the Tribunal's prompt reaction at the moments when Mr. Perisic needed assistance to attend the funeral. I would therefore like to thank both the registry and the secretariat who have contributed to this happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have many other matters to deal with and we have to combine, as usual, speed with efficiency and fairness. The second amended indictment was filed by the Prosecution. However, on reading the amended indictment it is clear that some amendments were made, which go beyond those that were authorised in the Chamber's decision of the 15th of May. And I will therefore give the Defence an opportunity to respond to those amendments, which exceed the authority in the decision of the 15th of May, and the Defence will have 30 days in which to submit any objections, those 30 days being from the receipt of the B/C/S version of the indictment and the Prosecution will have 14 days in which to reply. I turn next to pending motions. There is a Prosecution motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts concerning Sarajevo, and the Defence has filed two responses. I will deal with that later when I deal with adjudicated facts as a discrete subject. The Prosecution's supplemental 65 ter summary contains a witness Dragan Erdemovic. The Defence was to respond on the 31st of August but it does not appear that any such response was filed, and I'm to ask Mr. Lukic whether any response has been filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. It hasn't been filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm to say that in any event the Chamber will give a decision on this matter in due course. There is also a Defence motion for sanctions for failure to bring the accused to trial without undue delay. The Prosecution response was filed on the 23rd of August, 2007, and the Chamber will give a decision shortly on this matter. There is also a Prosecution motion relating to Rule 70, in respect of which the Prosecution has not yet received the required permission from the state concerned, and the Chamber will be monitoring this in the usual way. I turn next to disclosure. Rule 66(A)(i), supporting material to the indictment, there are no issues outstanding in this regard. 66(A)(ii), witness statements, there is an issue, I understand, relating to the redacted statements of protected witnesses MP-003, MP-004, and MP-014. The Defence has submitted that their testimony should be excluded, or, alternatively, that an order requiring copies of the redacted statements be provided within seven days. The Prosecution submitted at the 65 ter Conference yesterday that it had no statements relating to 003 and 004. In relation to 014, its submission was that disclosure would prejudice the identity of the witness, in violation of the existing protective measures that were issued on the 16th of November. The Defence has also notified the Chamber that it has not yet received a B/C/S version of the transcript of the accused's testimony -- accused's statement. Now, clearly there can be no obligation on the Prosecution to manufacture a statement for disclosure if no such statement exists. That is sufficient to deal with MP-003 and MP-004. As to MP-014, the existing protective measures are adequate to provide the statement to the Defence 30 days prior to, and no redacted statement should be required to be disclosed at this time. Therefore, in respect of MP-014, the Chamber's decision of November 16th stands. The Defence will get the unredacted statement of 014, 30 days prior to trial. The accused's statement is obviously an important document, and priority for its translation should be provided, and I will order the Prosecution to provide a B/C/S version of the transcript of the accused's statement by the 1st of December, 2007. I turn next to -- yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I just be heard on that. A transcript -- to prepare a transcript of a statement the defendant has had in his possession for two years will require us to consume five to six weeks of limited resources of translation resources that we have that we're trying to apply to untranslated exhibits. The Defence has applied to the registrar, that has been rejected. The Defence has the statement, Mr. Perisic has had the statement for, I think, at least two years. So the transcription of that statement is essentially a luxury that he is trying to impose on the Prosecution's office at the expense of what is more pressing and what is more pressing to us, and I think, Your Honour, more pressing to the Court would be to have the Defence receive in the fastest possible time the remaining outstanding translations. I just make those submissions to Your Honour because it will consume considerable resources and we do not have those resources and we have to then re-adjust our -- within the -- what we can provide to the Defence and we are trying our best to provide what the rules require and what the rules require are the translations not the transcript. He has the tape of the interview in his language. He has had that from -- shortly after --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He has had those the tape-recording of his statement since he was interviewed and I don't have the date, I'm trying to look that up, Your Honour, but it has been a couple of years. So sitting and making a transcript, applying our resources when Mr. Perisic could sit and make the same transcript seems to us, with due respect, Your Honour, to be a consumption of resources that are not required under the rules. He has his statement. So I make those submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For you, then, it is not a question of time within which to do this. It's that you say that you should not be required to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do. He has the statement, he has had the statement for years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Perisic did receive the audiotape in B/C/S, and indeed this was a long interview. What we insist upon and why we think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Are you able to say how long the -- or Mr. Harmon can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the interview lasted, I believe, six days. It is -- I think 600 pages. He has had the interview since approximately September the 5th, 2005. So in those -- that intervening period of time it seems to me that Mr. Perisic could have sat down and made his own transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I finish, please. I believe that we're talking about 500 pages, I can't be sure, but indeed the interview was long. But what we believe is that this document from the 65 ter list if it becomes an exhibit, will be used in Court quite often. It will be shown to a number of witnesses both on the Prosecution and the Defence sides, and many witnesses will come and testify in B/C/S. If we play audiotape to them instead of showing them that the transcript that will waste the Court's time. In the previous trials the interviews of a number of witnesses have been translated despite their length, and in trial they were used in the transcripted form. As you have told us before, this is a very important 65 ter document irrespective of the fact whether it will become an exhibit or not; most probably it will be used during trial. The problems with playing the audiotape or reading the English transcript and a vista by the interpretation will slow us down. It is a technical matter for this document to be translated into B/C/S before the beginning of trial and this is the main reason why we insist on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But as a matter of principle, whose responsibility is it. Mr. Harmon? I mean, suppose the transcript was just one page and not 500 or 600.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we normally do with suspect interviews is we play the audio recording, we have a transcript in English of the interview. That has -- the interview has been transcribed in B/C/S, so -- in the English, Your Honour. And so if we decide to use the interview as an exhibit and we are contemplating that possibility, if we are to use it, we would decide the best manner in which to do that because we're also concerned about efficiency. But right now, from our point of view, transcribing that whole interview in B/C/S, as I said, would take five to six weeks of our time. That's the best information I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but it doesn't answer the question that I'm asking. Whose responsibility is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If it is a one-page document in B/C/S, we would translate it, if it is a one-page document. But we make considerations, Your Honour, if it is a 600-page document, we sometimes excerpt only portions of that and we introduce portions of the transcript. We are doing that exercise now, Your Honour, in the course of reviewing documents that are voluminous. Book's passages, for example, we don't translate the whole book, we translate a paragraph that is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move on and come back to this at the end. Rule 68, mitigating exculpatory material. Of course, the provisions under Rule 68 impose an obligation that is ongoing. There are no issues here. 66(B), the Defence has notified the Chamber of a number of exhibits -- exhibit issues and translation issues. One, they say no English translation has been provided for 2721 exhibits which are in B/C/S. Two, no B/C/S translation for 488 exhibits in English. And they're particularly concerned that exhibits -- about exhibits to be offered through experts. And we'll come back to that later. Intercepts, 261 have now been identified, nine have no B/C/S translation and for 56 no English translation has been provided. Intelligence notes require English translation for those identified as exhibits. And the submission of the Defence is that translations are to be ordered or should be ordered before December the 1st, 2007 or the exhibits be struck from the list. It appears to the Chamber that it will be very difficult for the CLSS to make these translations a priority when other cases that are closer to trial have to be given greater priority. The Chamber will instruct the Prosecution to file a report by 31st October 2007, on the status of all outstanding translations with a projected completion date, and this includes the Rule 94 bis expert reports. Now pre-trial preparation, the use of 92 bis and Rule 92 ter. There have been a number of communications between the parties in relation to these matters. I don't consider it necessary for me to delve into them in any detail in this stage in the pre-trial proceedings. It is sufficient for me to say that motions relating to 92 bis, ter and quater, will be dealt with by the Trial Chamber that will hear the case. I turn next to adjudicated facts, agreed facts, and stipulations on the indictment. The parties filed a joint submission on agreements on matters of law on 1st May 2007. The parties filed a joint submission on agreements on matters of fact on 31st May 2007. Adjudicated facts, the Prosecution filed a motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts concerning Sarajevo, to which I have referred. The Defence filed two responses. This motion is currently pending, but I indicated on the 23rd of May that motions for admission of adjudicated facts will be determined by the Trial Chamber that will hear the case. The anticipated length of the trial, I was informed on the 23rd of May that the length of the trial will be approximately one year and a half. Now, I return to the question that we considered earlier and which I have not decided. I had originally said that the Prosecution was to provide a B/C/S version of the transcript of the accused's statement by 1st December 2007. I have heard submissions from both parties. Please put those submissions in writing, and I will give a decision on this matter early next week. Let us have those submissions by Friday. Mr. Lukic, did you hear? The submissions by Friday. At this stage, it is perhaps not necessary to set a date for another Status Conference, but I prefer to err on the side of precaution and I'm therefore going to set Tuesday, January the 15th, 2005 [sic]. And I'm to ask Mr. Lukic whether there is any matter that wishes to raise concerning the detention of the accused or his health or any other matter relating to the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the health condition of the accused, I can say that there are no problems. He is complying with all of the decisions of the Pre-Trial Chamber relative to his provisional release and he will continue to do so. I don't have any other issues to raise at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Only that the record typo, a typographical error on page 10, line 8 it says 2005. I think it should say 2008. And other than that, Your Honour, I have no other submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, going -- Tuesday, January 15th, 2008. Thank you very much for that correction. There being no other matter, the hearing is adjourned.
